title: Pruning LLMs Like a Physicist: Block Removal as an Ising Optimization Problem
gist: Multiverse Computing reformulates transformer block removal as a constrained binary optimization problem equivalent to an Ising glass, using a once-computed Hessian's off-diagonal couplings to rank prunings without benchmarking them. At 50% depth compression of Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct with no retraining the method holds MMLU at 76.9 versus 54.0 for the best block-influence baseline, and the approach transfers to hybrid Mamba2/attention/MoE architectures.

insights.claim: Existing block-removal methods that score each transformer block independently using magnitude, sensitivity or 'block influence' heuristics are mean-field approximations that discard the pairwise couplings between removal decisions.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for spotting where current model-compression tooling leaves quality on the table.
insights.quote: In physics terms these are mean-field methods: they treat each block as if its contribution were independent of the others
insights.locator: Why picking blocks is a many-body problem

insights.claim: Block selection is a combinatorial problem rather than a ranking problem, because the effect of removing any one transformer block depends on which other blocks are removed alongside it.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Any compression vendor selling a per-block importance score is solving the wrong problem at deep compression ratios.
insights.quote: That makes it a combinatorial problem, not a ranking problem
insights.locator: One of the cheapest ways to make a large language model faster

insights.claim: Assigning a binary keep/remove variable per block and taking a second-order Taylor expansion of the model's loss yields a Hessian whose diagonal captures standalone block importance and whose off-diagonal entries are exactly the pairwise couplings mean-field methods ignore.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: The mechanism is cheap and generic enough to be adopted by any inference-optimization stack.
insights.quote: The diagonal of that Hessian is how much each block matters on its own; the off-diagonal entries are exactly the pairwise couplings between blocks
insights.locator: The idea: turn block selection into an energy-minimization problem

insights.claim: Constraining removal to exactly M of N blocks makes the problem an Ising glass with conserved magnetization, where the fixed number of removed blocks plays the role of a fixed total spin.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Mapping to a canonical Hamiltonian is what unlocks decades of existing solver infrastructure for an ML problem.
insights.locator: That reformulation turns "which blocks should I remove?"

insights.claim: The spin-system energy is established as a strong proxy for downstream benchmark quality, meaning low-energy states correspond to high-performing pruned models and energy minimization and benchmark maximization become the same search.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Replaces expensive benchmark-in-the-loop search with a cheap scalar, collapsing the cost of compression R&D.
insights.quote: Minimizing energy and maximizing benchmark score become the same search.
insights.locator: The key property we establish

insights.claim: The full coupling matrix is computed just once from forward and backward passes on a small calibration dataset, after which evaluating any candidate pruning configuration is a single cheap energy calculation with no need to run the model.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: One-time fixed cost plus near-zero marginal cost per candidate is the economics that makes exhaustive search viable.
insights.quote: The Hessian, i.e. the full set of couplings, is computed just once, from forward and backward passes on a small calibration dataset.
insights.locator: The reason this is practical is cost

insights.claim: Because the couplings do not depend on the compression target, the same Hessian can be reused to solve for many different compression ratios without recomputation.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: One calibration run yields an entire family of compressed model sizes — attractive for serving multiple hardware tiers.
insights.locator: And because the couplings don’t depend on

insights.claim: Brute-force enumeration on a single GPU can check up to tens of billions of spin configurations, with the hardest tractable case of removing 8 of Llama-3.3-70B's 80 blocks (about 29 billion configurations) taking roughly two days.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Concrete compute cost for verification: two GPU-days is affordable, meaning this is deployable today without exotic hardware.
insights.quote: the hardest tractable case here, removing 8 of Llama-3.3-70B's 80 blocks (about 29 billion configurations), took roughly two days
insights.locator: Solving it: exact when you can

insights.claim: An open-source tabu solver reliably reaches the lowest-energy states in seconds even on the hardest cases verifiable against brute force, so the method scales to models where enumeration is impossible without requiring quantum hardware.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: The quantum framing is marketing-adjacent; a free classical solver does the work today, which lowers the adoption barrier.
insights.quote: We find that an open-source tabu solver reliably reaches the lowest-energy states in seconds, even on the hardest cases we can verify against brute force.
insights.locator: In its equivalent QUBO form

insights.claim: Unlike conventional combinatorial optimization where solvers are judged on finding the true ground state, this application only needs a handful of good low-energy states, a far easier bar that lets lightweight solvers succeed.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Reframes the solver requirement downward — a reason to doubt that quantum-annealing hardware is needed for this class of ML problem.
insights.quote: We don't actually need the ground state. What we need is a fast way to generate a handful of good low-energy states, and that is a far easier bar
insights.locator: There’s a subtle but important point here

insights.claim: The lowest-energy configuration is not always the best pruned model because energy is a strong but imperfect proxy for quality, so reading off the ground state plus low-lying excited states gives a spectrum of candidate prunings essentially for free.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Generating a candidate set rather than one answer is a cheap robustness upgrade for any proxy-driven optimization pipeline.
insights.quote: This turns out to be a feature, not a bug
insights.locator: Why the whole low-energy spectrum matters

insights.claim: For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at 16 of 32 blocks removed, the 17th excited state is the first configuration to propose removing a block near the beginning of the model, and after light retraining it outperforms the ground state across several benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that the accepted pruning heuristic discards the best configurations.
insights.locator: A concrete example: for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct

insights.claim: The common assumption that the best pruning is one consecutive chunk of middle-or-late transformer blocks is directly disproved by configurations that remove an early block and score better after retraining.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Invalidates a widely used shortcut in production pruning pipelines — a source of free quality for anyone who drops it.
insights.quote: That directly disproves the common assumption that the best pruning is one consecutive chunk of middle-or-late blocks
insights.locator: But the 17th excited state

insights.claim: At 40 of 80 blocks removed from Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct with no retraining, the constrained binary optimization method holds MMLU at 76.9 versus 54.0 for the block-influence baseline, against an original model score of 82.2.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Halving model depth while losing only ~5 MMLU points changes the cost curve for serving frontier-class open models.
insights.quote: At 40/80 (50% depth), CBO holds MMLU near 77 while the strongest baseline falls to the mid-50s.
insights.locator: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, no retraining

insights.claim: The advantage of coupling-aware pruning is concentrated at aggressive compression: up to 24 of 80 blocks removed the method is roughly on par with block influence, but it pulls decisively ahead at 32/80 and 40/80.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Only buyers pursuing deep compression get value here; at light compression incumbent heuristics are good enough.
insights.quote: At lighter compression the methods are comparable, which is expected: the couplings matter most when you're cutting deep.
insights.locator: Results

insights.claim: For Qwen3-14B at 12 of 40 blocks removed, the method leads block influence on MMLU by about 10 points.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: The gain is not Llama-specific, which matters for anyone standardizing on Qwen-family models.
insights.quote: For Qwen3-14B at 12/40 removed, CBO leads MMLU by about 10 points.
insights.locator: Results

insights.claim: Block removal makes the model literally shorter, so it buys predictable inference speedups on top of memory savings and stacks cleanly with quantization, low-rank compression, width pruning and distillation-based healing.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Compounding compression techniques multiply, so total achievable cost reduction per served token is larger than any single method suggests.
insights.quote: Because the model literally gets shorter, block removal (also called depth pruning) buys predictable inference speedups on top of the memory savings
insights.locator: One of the cheapest ways to make a large language model faster

insights.claim: Applied without retraining to NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-FP8, a hybrid interleaving Mamba2, attention and mixture-of-experts layers in a non-uniform pattern, the method beats block influence on AIME25 and GPQA when removing 2-3 MoE layers or 2 attention layers.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Method generality across architectures is what determines whether a compression vendor can serve the whole market as architectures fragment.
insights.locator: It generalizes beyond dense transformers

insights.claim: Redundancy in hybrid Mamba/attention/MoE models is real but unevenly distributed, with some expert layers far more disposable than others — a pattern only a coupled configuration-space search can locate.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Uneven redundancy means per-architecture compression ratios are not transferable rules of thumb; each model needs its own search.
insights.quote: redundancy in these hybrid models is real but unevenly distributed: some expert layers are far more disposable than others
insights.locator: The results also confirm

insights.claim: The formulation is architecture-agnostic because a coupling is a coupling regardless of what kind of block sits at each site, so nothing in the method assumes a homogeneous transformer stack.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Architecture-agnosticism is the durability argument for this IP as model designs keep diverging from dense transformers.
insights.quote: a coupling is a coupling regardless of what kind of block sits at each site
insights.locator: Block removal gets much harder on modern heterogeneous architectures

insights.claim: Multiverse Computing has open-sourced the code for this method and published the underlying paper, positioning block removal as one composable layer in a broader compression stack it sells rather than a standalone product.
insights.speaker: Antonio Tiene
insights.so_what: Open-sourcing the selection method while monetizing the full stack is the commercial pattern to watch in model-compression vendors.
insights.locator: Why this fits Multiverse Computing
